Cerebrospinal fluid amyloid and neurodegeneration biomarkers in the diagnosis and prognosis of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis: a multicohort observational study. Neurofilament light chain (NfL) is an established biomarker for amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS). However, it remains unclear whether biomarkers reflecting amyloid-β metabolism (Aβ), tau (phosphorylated tau, pTau), and astrogliosis (glial fibrillary acidic protein, GFAP) can complement NfL in clinical applications. It is also unclear how Alzheimer's disease (AD) co-pathology affects disease progression in ALS.

Cardiopulmonary exercise testing in children with cerebral palsy: Feasibility and the relationship between aerobic capacity and gross motor function: A pilot study. Children with cerebral palsy (CP) may exhibit reduced aerobic capacity. While the cardiopulmonary exercise test (CPET) is the gold standard for determining aerobic capacity, motor disorders and accompanying disturbances make its application challenging. The 6-minute walk test (6-MWT) may offer a practical alternative.

[Acute Stroke Rehabilitation:Clinical Recommendations and Practical Guidance for Stroke Specialists]. Acute stroke rehabilitation is essential for preventing disuse syndrome and other post-stroke complications, promoting neurological recovery, improving activities of daily living, and facilitating social reintegration. However, acute stroke rehabilitation programs and service-delivery systems vary considerably among institutions in Japan. To address this issue, the Japan Stroke Society established a project team to promote the standardization and equitable provision of acute stroke rehabilitation. Based on a nationwide cross-sectional web-based questionnaire survey of 959 primary stroke centers and a literature review, the first clinical recommendations for acute stroke rehabilitation were made publicly available on the Japan Stroke Society's website in June 2023. In this article, we summarize the key concepts and clinical considerations of the acute stroke recommendations with a focus on issues relevant to stroke specialists. In-bed exercises and dysphagia screening should be promptly initiated after admission. Mobilization is generally appropriate 24-48 h after stroke onset, whereas very early, high-dose mobilization within 24 h should be performed cautiously. In selected patients with acute complications, rehabilitation training may be continued provided that neurological symptoms and systemic conditions remain stable. Adequate training duration and frequency, provision of rehabilitation on nonworking days, early dysphagia management, and nutritional support are also important components of acute stroke rehabilitation. Safe and effective rehabilitation requires a multidisciplinary approach and standardized institutional protocols. Stroke specialists should assess neurological and systemic stability, complications, comorbidities, and stroke pathophysiology to determine when rehabilitation training and mobilization can be initiated safely.
